details:
**Venus of Urbino**
Titian's most famous painting (1538), showing a nude woman reclining on a white bed and gazing at the viewer while holding a small bouquet of flowers. A small dog, often read as a symbol of fidelity, sleeps curled at her feet, and in the background two maids rummage through a cassone (marriage chest). It was the main model for Manet's Olympia.

**Bacchus and Ariadne**
A painting for the Duke of Ferrara in which the wine god Bacchus leaps from his chariot, drawn by two cheetahs, toward Ariadne, who has been abandoned by Theseus, whose ship sails away in the distance. Bacchus's revelers include a man wrestling with snakes and a satyr child dragging a calf's head. A ring of eight stars in the upper left represents the crown Bacchus will turn into a constellation for her.

**Sacred and Profane Love**
An allegorical painting showing two similar-looking women seated at either end of a stone fountain carved like a sarcophagus: one richly clothed as a bride in white, the other nude. Cupid reaches into the water between them, and the side of the fountain shows a relief of a flogging. The figures have been read as two forms of Venus, and one theory identifies them as Polia and Venus.

**Giorgione**
The Venetian painter, Titian's teacher and early collaborator, who shaped his rich use of color. Titian completed Giorgione's Sleeping Venus, painting its landscape, and that work was the model for the Venus of Urbino. The Pastoral Concert was long attributed to Giorgione but is now often given to Titian.

**Pesaro Madonna**
An altarpiece in Venice's Frari church, painted for Jacopo Pesaro. It is daringly asymmetrical: the Madonna and Child sit off-center to the right, while a large red banner bearing the papal and Pesaro coats of arms balances the left side. An armored soldier leads in a turbaned Turkish prisoner, and the Christ Child turns toward Saint Francis.

**Poesie for Philip II**
Titian's name ("poesie," poems) for a series of mythological paintings, drawn largely from Ovid, that he made for King Philip II of Spain and regarded as the painted equivalent of poetry. The series includes Danaë, Venus and Adonis, Diana and Actaeon, Diana and Callisto, Perseus and Andromeda, and The Rape of Europa. The poesie were reunited in a 2021 exhibition that ended at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, which owns The Rape of Europa.

**Diana and Actaeon / The Death of Actaeon**
In Diana and Actaeon, the hunter Actaeon pushes aside a red curtain and stumbles on the goddess Diana and her nymphs bathing at a stone fountain, while a stag's skull foreshadows his fate. In the later Death of Actaeon, Diana shoots her bow as Actaeon, now with a stag's head, is torn apart by his own hounds.

**The Rape of Europa**
One of the poesie, showing Jupiter disguised as a white bull carrying the princess Europa out to sea as she clings to one of his horns. It is held by the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston.

**Danaë**
A series of paintings, made in several versions, of the mythical princess Danaë reclining as Jupiter visits her as a shower of gold. Some versions include Cupid, and others an old nursemaid trying to catch the coins.

**Allegory of Prudence**
A late painting showing three human heads, an old man, a middle-aged man, and a youth, often identified as Titian, his son Orazio, and a young relative. Below them are the heads of a wolf, a lion, and a dog, representing past, present, and future, and the work carries a Latin inscription about prudence.

**Assumption of the Virgin (Frari)**
Titian's huge altarpiece for the high altar of the Frari church in Venice. The Virgin, in a red dress, rises on a cloud borne by cherubs into a brilliant golden glow where God the Father waits, while the apostles below gesture upward in amazement.

**The Flaying of Marsyas**
One of Titian's last works, showing the satyr Marsyas hanging upside down from a tree, his panpipes hanging nearby, as Apollo flays him for daring to challenge the god to a musical contest. A small dog laps up his blood beneath him.

**Equestrian Portrait of Charles V (Battle of Mühlberg)**
A portrait of Holy Roman Emperor Charles V in armor on a rearing black horse, painted in Augsburg to commemorate his 1547 victory over Protestant forces at Mühlberg. It helped found the tradition of the royal equestrian portrait; the writer Pietro Aretino had helped connect Titian with Charles V.

**Pastoral Concert**
A painting of two clothed young men, one a lute player in red, sitting in a landscape with two nude women, one of whom pours water from a glass jug into a stone well. Once attributed to Giorgione and now often to Titian, it inspired Manet's Luncheon on the Grass.

**Man with a Blue Sleeve**
An early portrait of a man seen from the right side, dominated by a huge, quilted, blue-gray sleeve that juts out toward the viewer over a stone ledge. It was once thought to show the poet Ludovico Ariosto and may be a self-portrait of Titian.
